Here's how the three compare, what each does best, and which makes the most sense for how you work.

Google and Microsoft are built around ecosystem integration. Proton is built around keeping your data yours, without sacrificing productivity tools.

Recent findings suggest that google Workspace is the go-to suite for startups, agencies and freelancers, and for good reason. Gmail, Drive, Docs, Sheets, Calendar and Meet work together seamlessly, and several people can edit the same file in real time without emailing versions back and forth.

Industry observers note that google encrypts data at rest and in transit, and offers client-side encryption on eligible editions. But that extra layer requires higher-tier plans and configuration, so in the default experience Google holds the keys. A password manager and VPN aren't part of the suite.

Best for: Teams whose top priorities are real-time collaboration and third-party integrations.

According to recent reports, if your work runs on Word, Excel and Outlook, Microsoft 365 needs little introduction. Business Standard includes full desktop apps, and Excel remains the benchmark for heavy spreadsheet work.

According to recent reports, that breadth comes with complexity. Licensing, permissions and device management can eat into time a small team or solo developer would rather spend shipping. And like Google, Microsoft's everyday productivity experience isn't built around end-to-end encryption, while Copilot and advanced security features add cost.

Proton Workspace starts from a different premise. Instead of building a productivity suite and adding privacy features on top, Proton built privacy into the foundation, then delivered the everyday tools around it.

Everything is managed from one admin console, with one bill.

This is the core difference. Proton uses zero-access encryption: your data is encrypted before it reaches Proton's servers, and Proton never holds the keys. Proton can't read your data. Not won't. Can't.

Is Proton Workspace a good alternative to Google Workspace for developers?

Yes, for developers who prioritize privacy and cost. It covers email, storage, documents, spreadsheets and video calls, adds a password manager and VPN, and costs $12.99/user/month versus $14 for Google Workspace Business Standard.

Can Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 read my email and files?

Sources indicate that by default, yes. Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 hold the encryption keys, and their default terms give them access to your data.

Can Proton read my email and files?

No. Zero-access encryption means Proton never holds the keys to your stored data. Emails between Proton owners are end-to-end encrypted automatically, and you can send password-protected encrypted emails to anyone.

According to recent reports, yes. Proton's apps are open source and independently audited.

Can I use Proton Mail with my existing email client?

Does Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 use my data to train AI?

It can. If your plan allows Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 to hold the encryption keys, they can access your data and use it to train their integrated AI models.

Does Proton use my data to train AI?

No. Proton can't read your data, so it can't use it for AI training.

Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 are mature, capable platforms, and if your work depends on advanced Excel or a deep web of Google integrations, there's a good case for using them.

But if you're a freelancer or a developer or running a small team, Proton Workspace is the stronger choice. You get the same core tools for less money, a password manager and VPN you'd otherwise pay for separately, and encryption that keeps client data, code and credentials readable only by you.

You don't have to take that on faith, either. The code is open source, and the trial is free.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, here’s an overview of how the OlympicCoder models stack up against various instruction fine-tuned and reasoning models.
  • Read on to learn how we built the dataset, benchmark and models!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the last few weeks, we have focused our efforts on reproducing the competitive programming (code reasoning) aspects of the DeepSeek-R1 recipe.

In this post, we are excited to share:.

According to recent reports, here’s an overview of how the OlympicCoder models stack up against various instruction fine-tuned and reasoning models. We find that training models on CodeForces-CoTs produces top-tier performance, with OlympicCoder-32B outperforming all open-weight models we tested, including some that are over 100x larger 🤯.

Read on to learn how we built the dataset, benchmark and models!

International Olympiad in Informatics (IOI).

Sources indicate that codeForces is one of the most popular websites among competitive programmers, hosting regular contests where participants must solve challenging algorithmic optimization problems. The challenging nature of these problems makes them an interesting dataset to improve and test models’ code reasoning capabilities.

While previous efforts such as DeepMind’s CodeContests dataset have compiled a large number of CodeForces problems, today we are releasing our own open-r1/codeforces dataset, with more than 10k problems covering the very first contests all the way to 2025, ~3k of which were not included in DeepMind’s dataset. Additionally, for around 60% of the problems, we have included the editorial, which is an explanation, written by the contest organizers, explaining the correct solution. You will also find 3 correct solutions per problem extracted from the official website.

Furthermore, we are releasing open-r1/codeforces-cots, which contains chain of thought generations produced by DeepSeek-R1 on these problems, where we asked the model to produce solutions in C++ (the main language used in competitive programming) and Python, totaling close to 100k samples.

Industry observers note that we fine-tuned Qwen2.5 Coder Instruct 7B and 32B on this dataset, resulting in our OlympicCoder-7B and OlympicCoder-32B models. You will find more details on these models further along in the blogpost.

While datasets like DeepMind’s contests and others containing competitive programming problems include test cases and claim to be verifiable, these test cases are often a small subset of the full suite used on contest websites. CodeForces, in particular, caps displayed test cases at ~500 characters, which means that these datasets only contain the shorter, easier test cases that fit into this limit.

As an example, we took 7 problems for which the R1 generated solution passed all the public test cases and tried submitting them to the CodeForces platform:.

Recent findings suggest that although they passed the shorter tests, every single one of these solutions failed on the full test set. This underscores the need for upcoming fully verifiable competitive programming dataset. While we initiative to try model-based solutions to generate and validate additional challenging tests that may be added to our CodeForces dataset in the future, for now we went looking for fully available problem data elsewhere.

The International Olympiad in Informatics (IOI) is one of five international science olympiads (if you are familiar with AIME, IOI is the programming equivalent of IMO, for which the very best students who take part in AIME are invited) and tests a very select group of high school students (4 per country) in complex algorithmic problems.

The problems are extremely challenging, and the full test sets are available and released under a permissive (CC-BY) license. This means that IOI is the perfect dataset to test a model's code reasoning capabilities.

In IOI, each problem has several subtasks, each with different input constraints. To solve a subtask, a submission needs to pass all of its test cases within the (strict) time limits. While the final subtask is usually the “full problem”, some subtasks effectively describe a much easier (more constrained) problem, and contestants very often target specific subtasks to get partial scores instead of just trying to solve the full problem (perfect scores are relatively rare).

Recent findings suggest that following a recent OpenAI paper where o1 live competed at IOI’2024 (the last iteration), we similarly processed all problems from IOI’2024 (as well as previous IOIs up until 2020), and split them into their subtasks, such that each prompt would ask models to solve one specific subtask. We release the processed problem statements, as well as all grading/checker files required to run them and test cases in open-r1/ioi and open-r1/ioi-test-cases.

We created custom code to run solutions (many problems have complicated setups, requiring a “manager” process communicating with several processes running the user submission and special checkers to validate solutions) and to grade according to IOI rules, which is available at https://github.com/huggingface/ioi, and evaluated over 40 leading reasoning models on IOI’2024.

In a recent development, at IOI, contestants have a 50 submission limit per problem. We generated 50 submissions for each subtask and then applied a selection strategy similar to the one used by OpenAI to get scores under contest conditions for each problem. Results can be found below, where the horizontal lines represent the threshold for bronze, silver and gold models from real contest data. While o1 comes very close to bronze, ultimately no model would reach the medal threshold (50th percentile of contestants).

Our OlympicCoder models (in red), do fairly well compared to other frontier models, even surpassing some closed source models (in gold) such as claude-3.7-sonnet-thinking, and OlympicCoder-32B even outperforms o1-mini and DeepSeek-R1, the model we distilled from, on the 50 submission limit setting.

An important note is that our submission strategy may penalize non reasoning models, such as Qwen-2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct, OlympicCoder-32B’s base model. To simulate real contest conditions, in which a submission’s score is only known after it is actually submitted, we employed a round robin submission strategy similar to the one employed by OpenAI for o1-ioi: we start by submitting a solution that targets the last subtask of the problem, then one targeting the second to last, and so on, only evaluating a solution when it is picked for submission. We skip over submissions targeting subtasks that have already been solved by previously selected submissions, and within each targeted subtask we prefer submissions from longer generations — which is a criteria that makes sense for reasoning models, but less so for other models.

If we remove the 50 submission limit (which would place us outside the contest conditions), and evaluate all submissions we generated (50 per subtask), we obtain the following results:.

Recent findings suggest that while creating the OlympicCoder models, we ran a large number of SFT experiments to understand the role of various filters applied to the CodeForces dataset. We found the following subsets of open-r1/codeforces-cots gave the best overall performance:.

Note that we only focused on the C++ solutions, but blending in the Python solutions would likely boost performance even further.

It has been revealed that we used LiveCodeBench as a test bed for our models and then ran the best performing checkpoints through the much harder IOI benchmark. We tested various hyperparameter configurations to train our models and settled on the following:.

Below we share some lessons we learned from tuning the Qwen2.5 Coder models on R1 reasoning traces.

Sample packing is a widely used method to efficiently process variable-length sequences and accelerate training. As shown in the figure below, the way this works concatenating training samples (coloured) into equal sized chunks that removes the need to use padding tokens (gray) across batches:.

With packing, samples can overlap across the boundaries of each chunk, but in practice this doesn’t matter too much if most of the samples are much smaller than the chunk size.

Recent findings suggest that however, for the reasoning traces we distilled from R1, we wondered whether packing could hurt performance because many traces are long and the fraction of clipped answers could be high. This means it may be difficult to train the model to attend to long context information, particularly when the question and answer have been packed into different chunks.

As shown in the striking figure below, we found that packing substantially hurts the model’s performance: with packing, the model is barely able to solve problems from LiveCodebench, but without packing, the performance improves over several epochs before plateauing out:.

We suspect this stark difference is accentuated by the fact that our training sets only consist of C++ solutions, while LiveCodeBench only evaluates performance on Python. Nevertheless, we found that across all datasets we ablated, packing was consistently worse.

Recent findings suggest that for most SFT experiments that we’ve run with Qwen models, a learning rate of 2e-5 is typically good enough to get strong performance. However, when applying SFT with reasoning data to an existing instruct model, we found that significant performance gains could be had by using a much larger learning rate of 4e-5. As shown in the figure below, the difference across each doubling of the learning rate amounted to almost 10 points improvement on LiveCodeBench!

Sources indicate that when we created the solutions_w_editorials subset of open-r1/codeforces-cots, our intuition was that by providing R1 with the problem and solution, we would obtain better reasoning traces. Surprisingly, this intuition was not borne out during evaluation, with the naive sampling from problem statements giving a modest, yet consistent boost during training:.

While vibe testing some of our models, we encountered a peculiar phenomenon: if prompted with in-domain queries (like competitive coding), the model would emit the expected long CoT within and tokens, followed by the final answer. However, for out-of-domain queries like “What is the capital of Switzerland”, the model would revert back to the behaviour of the original instruct model!

Here’s an example of a simple query failing to return the long CoT:.

According to recent reports, assistant: 2. It is one of the simplest mathematical addition problems. 1 + 1 equals 2. This problem is often used as a riddle or puzzle, particularly in job interviews or online tests to determine a candidate's ability to solve problems promptly. While it may seem obvious to most people, it can be a useful question for employers to assess critical thinking and problem-solving skills. Additionally, it is an notable concept in mathematics and forms the basis for more complex arithmetic operations. So next time someone asks you what 1+1 is, you can confidently state that it is 2!

In this solution, we define a function add_numbers that takes two parameters a and b and returns their sum. We then call this function with 1 and 1, storing the result in the variable result, which is then printed. This demonstrates a straightforward way to compute and display the sum of two integers. The example serves as a simple yet effective illustration of basic arithmetic operations in Python.

However, if we prefill the assistant's response with the desired behaviour emerges:.

According to recent reports, assistant: Okay, I need to answer the question "What is 1+1?" Let's see. Oh right, 1 plus 1 equals 2. But wait, maybe there's more to it. Like, what if someone asks in a different way? Or perhaps considering other number bases? Like in base 10 it's 2, but in binary it's 10. Hmm, but the question is straightforward. The user probably expects the simple answer. So the correct answer here is 2. Should I just state that? Yes, 1 + 1 is equal to 2. Is there anything else you'd like to know about this calculation?

Sources indicate that this suggests that when distilling reasoning traces into an existing post-trained model, one should enforce prefilling by default in the final model’s chat template. Incidentally, this is also what DeepSeek does with their distilled models and the behaviour above may be the reason why. (It is also amusing to speculate whether hitting the “think” button on popular chat UIs is simply prefilling the assistant response 🙂).

Combining all these lessons produced OlympicCoder-7B, which matches the performance of DeepSeek’s distilled model and significantly improves on the base Qwen2.5-Coder one:.

In a recent development, throughout the training of OlympicCoder-7B, we found DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 was sufficient to train each model with 32k context on a single node of 8 x H100s. However, when we tried scaling up our recipe to 32B, we ran into a host of memory concerns. In particular, our runs would OOM once the context was scaled beyond 20k tokens, even on 16 nodes 😢. This wasn’t ideal as 20% of the CodeForces-CoTs traces are larger than 20k tokens, which means they would get truncated during training.

The root of the problem is that transformers and trl do not yet support context parallelism, although see this issue to track progress.

In the meantime, we explored a variety of memory saving techniques and found that combining FSDP with the paged_adamw_8bit optimizer allowed us to scale the context to 22,528 tokens: still not ideal, but only 9% of the data was truncated.

Industry observers note that recent progress has been made to improve the implementation of GRPO in TRL, bringing enhancements that further boost efficiency, scalability, and resource utilization. Here’s a summary of the most important changes since the last update:.

One of the main bottlenecks of GRPO is the same as for any online method: generation takes time. A key way to make GRPO more sample-efficient is to reuse generated samples multiple times during optimization instead of discarding them after a single use. This technique was actually introduced a long time ago with PPO.

For GRPO, the number of times a sample is reused is denoted as μ.

It is now possible to reuse generated samples multiple times, significantly speeding up the process.

Sources indicate that however, be cautious—if μ is too large, it can negatively impact learning. Based on our experience, a good balance is between 2 and 4.

When training a model, not all rewards are equally important. For example, we may want the model to prioritize correctness over formatting, rather than treating both aspects equally.

In a recent development, to address this, it is now possible to assign different weights to different rewards, allowing finer control over the optimization process. By adjusting these weights, we can guide the model to focus more on the aspects that matter most for a given task.

Several smaller but impactful improvements have been made to GRPO:.

Based on our findings, the optimal filtering method depends heavily on the training token budget. For shorter runs, stricter verification methods offer significant advantages. As a general recommendation, we recommend combining llama verification with math_verify—as done in the LorMV dataset.

Welcome Gemma 3: Google's all new multimodal, multilingual, long context open LLM

📅 12 Mar 2025 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1712 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, today Google releases Gemma 3, a newly introduced iteration of their Gemma family of models.
  • All the models are on the Hub and tightly integrated with the Hugging Face ecosystem.
  • Both pre-trained and instruction tuned models are released.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, today Google releases Gemma 3, a newly introduced iteration of their Gemma family of models. The models range from 1B to 27B parameters, have a context window up to 128k tokens, can accept images and text, and support 140+ languages.

Try out Gemma 3 now 👉🏻 Gemma 3 Space.

All the models are on the Hub and tightly integrated with the Hugging Face ecosystem.

Both pre-trained and instruction tuned models are released. Gemma-3-4B-IT beats Gemma-2-27B IT, while Gemma-3-27B-IT beats Gemini 1.5-Pro across benchmarks.

Sources indicate that gemma 3 is Google's latest iteration of open weight LLMs. It comes in four sizes, 1 billion, 4 billion, 12 billion, and 27 billion parameters with base (pre-trained) and instruction-tuned versions. Gemma 3 goes multimodal! The 4, 12, and 27 billion parameter models can process both images and text, while the 1B variant is text only.

The input context window length has been increased from Gemma 2’s 8k to 32k for the 1B variants, and 128k for all others. As is the case with other VLMs (vision-language models), Gemma 3 generates text in response to the user inputs, which may consist of text and, optionally, images. Example uses include question answering, analyzing image content, summarizing documents, etc.

Industry observers note that while these are multimodal models, one can use it as a text only model (as an LLM) without loading the vision encoder in memory. We will talk about this in more detail later in the inference section.

The three core enhancements in Gemma 3 over Gemma 2 are:.

Sources indicate that in this section, we will cover the technical details that lead to these enhancements. It is interesting to start with the knowledge of Gemma 2 and explore what was necessary to make these models even better. This exercise will help you think like the Gemma team and appreciate the details!

Scaling context length to 128k tokens could be achieved efficiently without training models from scratch. Instead, models are pretrained with 32k sequences, and only the 4B, 12B, and 27B models are scaled to 128k tokens at the end of pretraining, saving significant compute. Positional embeddings, like RoPE, are adjusted—upgraded from a 10k base frequency in Gemma 2 to 1M in Gemma 3—and scaled by a factor of 8 for longer contexts.

Recent findings suggest that KV Cache management is optimized using Gemma 2’s sliding window interleaved attention. Hyperparameters are tuned to interleave 5 local layers with 1 global layer (previously 1:1) and reduce the window size to 1024 tokens (down from 4096). Crucially, memory savings are achieved without degrading perplexity.

Gemma 3 models use SigLIP as an image encoder, which encodes images into tokens that are ingested into the language model. The vision encoder takes as input square images resized to 896x896. Fixed input resolution makes it more difficult to process non-square aspect ratios and high-resolution images. To address these limitations during inference, the images can be adaptively cropped, and each crop is then resized to 896x896 and encoded by the image encoder. This algorithm, called pan and scan, effectively enables the model to zoom in on smaller details in the image.

Similar to PaliGemma, attention in Gemma 3 works differently for text and image inputs. Text is handled with one-way attention, where the model focuses only on previous words in a sequence. Images, on the other hand, get full attention with no masks, allowing the model to look at every part of the image in a bidirectional manner, giving it a complete, unrestricted understanding of the visual input.

One can see in the figure below that the image tokens are provided with bi-directional attention (the entire square is lit up) while the text tokens have causal attention. It also highlights how attention works with the sliding window algorithm.

Sources indicate that to make a LLM multilingual, the pretraining dataset incorporates more languages. The dataset of Gemma 3 has double the amount of multilingual data to improve language coverage.

To account for the changes, the tokenizer is the same as that of Gemini 2.0. It is a SentencePiece tokenizer with 262K entries. The new tokenizer significantly improves the encoding of Chinese, Japanese and Korean text, at the expense of a slight increase of the token counts for English and Code.

For the curious mind, here is the technical report on Gemma 3, to dive deep into the enhancements.

The LMSys Elo score is a number that ranks language models based on how well they perform in head-to-head competitions, judged by human preferences. On LMSys Chatbot Arena, Gemma 3 27B IT reports an Elo score of 1339, and ranks among the top 10 best models, including leading closed ones. The Elo is comparable to o1-preview and is above other non-thinking open models. This score is achieved with Gemma 3 working on text-only inputs, like the other LLMs in the table.

Gemma 3 has been evaluated across benchmarks like MMLU-Pro (27B: 67.5), LiveCodeBench (27B: 29.7), and Bird-SQL (27B: 54.4), showing competitive performance compared to closed Gemini models. Tests like GPQA Diamond (27B: 42.4) and MATH (27B: 69.0) highlight its reasoning and math skills, while FACTS Grounding (27B: 74.9) and MMMU (27B: 64.9) demonstrate strong factual accuracy and multimodal abilities. However, it lags in SimpleQA (27B: 10.0) for basic facts. When compared to Gemini 1.5 models, Gemma 3 is often close—and sometimes better—proving its value as an accessible, high-performing option.

Prompt Management in TypeScript: LangSmith vs Git vs 3 Open-Source Registries

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1724 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • Every prompt registry we tested can change a prompt in a running TypeScript app, roll it back, and give production and staging different versions.
  • Sources indicate that we tested all of this with one small app and one prompt, which has a condition and a loop.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

In a recent development, weekly. Free. One click to leave.

Every prompt registry we tested can change a prompt in a running TypeScript app, roll it back, and give production and staging different versions. LangSmith's prompt hub, Langfuse, Phoenix and AcruxCore all passed those three tests. The real differences show up elsewhere: which template syntax each one accepts, how many npm packages it pulls in, how long a change takes to reach the app, and what happens when the registry is down.

Sources indicate that we tested all of this with one small app and one prompt, which has a condition and a loop. Git files served as the baseline. Every number below comes from a recorded run.

Most teams start with prompts in code: a template string, or a .txt file next to the code that uses it. That works until a product manager wants to change one sentence, and the change has to wait for a full release.

Industry observers note that A prompt registry moves the text out of the deploy. The app fetches the prompt by name and by a label such as production. You change which version the label points to, and the app picks up the latest text without a deploy.

It has been revealed that langSmith's prompt hub is the best-known registry, but it is not the only one. Several of the LangSmith alternatives also manage prompts, and three of them are open source and self-hostable: Langfuse, Phoenix and AcruxCore. We covered how those tools handle tracing in Self-Hosted LangSmith Alternatives: 4 Tools Tested on One TypeScript Agent. This article covers prompts only.

Recent findings suggest that every tool got the same prompt, support-reply. Its template takes three variables: a customer name, a blueprint, and a list of help articles. It has one condition: a priority line appears only for premium customers. It also has one loop: one line per help article. In Jinja2 syntax, the template looks like this:.

Sources indicate that one help article contains the text Settings > Export. We included it on purpose, to catch any tool that HTML-escapes > into >.

Every tool then ran the same sequence from a TypeScript script:.

Industry observers note that each tool used its own documented TypeScript SDK. The four registries passed all six steps. The rest of this article covers how each one got there, and what it cost.

Sources indicate that keeping prompts in the repository costs almost nothing. The template sits in prompts/support-reply.njk, and nunjucks, the JavaScript port of Jinja2, renders it:.

The autoescape: false line matters. Our first version called nunjucks.renderString() directly, and the test failed. The default environment HTML-escapes its output, so Settings > Export reached the model as Settings > Export. Escaping is correct for web pages and wrong for prompts.

According to recent reports, git gives you full Jinja2, code review on every prompt change, and history in the same place as the code. What it can't do is change a prompt in a running app. Every edit, and every rollback, waits for a deploy.

Sources indicate that langSmith stores a prompt as a serialized LangChain object (ChatPromptTemplate), not as plain text. LangSmith's own documentation claims you must use the LangChain npm package to pull prompts in TypeScript (Manage prompts programmatically). So a plain TypeScript app that uses the openai package still needs langchain and @langchain/core:.

Those three packages installed 23 packages and 70 MB. Most of the size is @langchain/* (27 MB) and js-tiktoken (22 MB).

According to recent reports, templates. In TypeScript, LangChain accepts f-string and mustache templates. Mustache sections ({{#docs}}…{{/docs}}) handled our loop. Mustache has no ==, though, so the premium check became an is_premium boolean computed in code. We also tried templateFormat: "jinja2", which LangChain's Python package supports. In TypeScript it threw DEFAULT_PARSER_MAPPING[templateFormat] is not a function.

Labels and rollback. production and staging are reserved tags, and the documentation moves them in the UI. The langsmith JavaScript client has no public method that moves a tag. Our script called the same REST route the SDK uses internally (POST /api/v1/repos/-//tags). It worked, but it is not a documented API.

Recent findings suggest that caching. The SDK caches prompts for 300 seconds by default. In our test, a running app saw the new version 300 seconds after we moved the tag.

According to recent reports, langfuse's TypeScript client is one package, @langfuse/client. It installed 5 packages and 8 MB:.

Creating a version, moving a label and reading by label are all public SDK calls: prompt.create, prompt.enhancement and prompt.get (Get started with prompt management).

In a recent development, templates. The documentation reveals only {{variable}} substitution. But compile() calls the mustache library, so sections worked for our loop. The type signature accepts only string values, so passing a list needed a cast. The Langfuse UI colours the section tags red, and it lists title and body as the prompt's variables, not docs or is_premium. We would not depend on behaviour the documentation doesn't promise. When we sent the Jinja2 version instead, Langfuse returned the {% if %} and {% for %} tags unchanged, with no error. The model would have received them as text.

Industry observers note that caching. The cache time is 60 seconds by default (Caching). Our app saw the change after 62 seconds. Langfuse is also the only client with a fallback option: a prompt string the SDK uses when it cannot reach the server on a cold start.

Sources indicate that phoenix's TypeScript client fetches a prompt by name and tag, and toSDK() converts it into the message format the openai package expects. Phoenix templates only replace variables, so the condition and the loop have to run in your code before rendering:.

That is 16 lines, against 6 to 8 for the other registries. All the extra lines are template logic that now lives in the app.

Templates. Phoenix offers MUSTACHE, F_STRING and NONE formats (Prompts reference). Even in MUSTACHE mode, though, rendering is a plain replacement of {{name}}. When we sent mustache sections, they came back unchanged, with no error.

It has been revealed that errors. getPrompt() catches every error, logs it and returns null. You can see this in the client source, src/utils/getPromptBySelector.ts. A missing prompt and an unreachable server look the same to your code, which is why the snippet checks for null.

Size and caching. The client installed 57 packages and 90 MB. Most of that is OpenTelemetry, which comes in through its @arizeai/phoenix-otel dependency. The client has no prompt cache, so every render is a network call. That is also why a label change showed up immediately: 0 seconds in our test.

AcruxCore stores Jinja2 templates and renders them on the server with nunjucks. The SDK sends the variables and gets back finished messages:.

The template from the test section works as it is, condition and loop included, with no is_premium flag computed in code. A label is called an alias here, and promoteAlias() moves it (Manage prompts via the SDK). The SDK installed 3 packages and 12 MB. Most of the 12 MB is one OpenTelemetry package, @opentelemetry/semantic-conventions.

In a recent development, templates. Jinja2 only. When we committed the mustache version, AcruxCore rejected it at commit time with Template parse error: unexpected token: #. That is a clear error, but it also means that moving mustache prompts from LangSmith or Langfuse requires rewriting them.

We sent the same two templates, a Jinja2 one and a mustache one, to each tool's own renderer:.

According to recent reports, the rows that matter most are the ones where the tags were left in the output, because those failures produce no error. The model receives raw template syntax, and the only symptom is a strange answer. Whatever tool you pick, test one prompt with logic in it before you move the rest.

Recent findings suggest that putting logic in the template is not automatically better. It lets someone change the condition without a deploy. It also lets them break the condition without a deploy. Keeping logic in code, as Phoenix forces you to do, puts every branch under code review and in your tests.

A registry is a new runtime dependency, so we tested an outage. The app reached each registry through a local proxy, and we switched the proxy off. A separate process then started while the registry was still unreachable.

In a recent development, langSmith, Langfuse and AcruxCore keep serving the last good version while the registry is down, even after the cache time has passed. The risk is a cold start: a fresh container or a serverless function that boots during the outage. Langfuse's fallback option is the built-in answer to that. With the other tools, keep a copy of each prompt in your code as a fallback, which brings back part of the Git setup.

According to recent reports, keep prompts in Git if engineers make every prompt change and your deploys are quick. Set autoescape: false, and you get Jinja2, reviews and history for free.

Use LangSmith's prompt hub if you already use LangChain, or already trace with LangSmith. If your app doesn't use LangChain, budget for the extra dependency and for the tag moves that only the UI supports.

It has been revealed that use Langfuse if you want a small client, a local compile(), and a fallback for cold starts. Keep to {{variable}} substitution unless you are comfortable relying on mustache behaviour that the documentation doesn't promise.

It has been revealed that use Phoenix if you already use it for tracing, or if you prefer all template logic in code. Remember the null check, and that every render is a network call.

Use AcruxCore if you want real conditions and loops in the template and rendering on the server. Expect one network call per newly introduced set of variables, and a personal API key for writes.

Before you choose, run one of your own prompts with real logic in it through the tool's SDK, not through its playground. Two of the four registries we tested failed on template syntax without any error, and an SDK run is where you would see that.

Xet is on the Hub

📅 18 Mar 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1344 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Click here to read about joining the Xet waitlist (or head over to join immediately).
  • Over the past few weeks, Hugging Face’s Xet Team took a major step forward by migrating the first Model and Dataset repositories off LFS and to Xet storage.
  • This marks one of many steps to fulfill Hugging Face’s vision for the Hub by empowering AI builders to build, iterate, and collaborate more effectively on massive models and datasets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Click here to read about joining the Xet waitlist (or head over to join immediately).

Over the past few weeks, Hugging Face’s Xet Team took a major step forward by migrating the first Model and Dataset repositories off LFS and to Xet storage.

This marks one of many steps to fulfill Hugging Face’s vision for the Hub by empowering AI builders to build, iterate, and collaborate more effectively on massive models and datasets. If you're interested in deeper dives on the technology itself, check out the following posts:.

But this post isn't about the core technology. It's a behind-the-scenes view of getting Xet on the Hub; taking you through our proof-of-concept to the first migration of repositories.

In a recent development, the migration shifted ~6% of the Hub’s download traffic onto Xet infrastructure, validating several integral components and testing integrations with the myriad of ways repositories are accessed (e.g., via local development environments, different libraries, CI systems, cloud platforms, etc.). With nearly two million developers working on over two million public repositories, it’s real-world usage that’s the ultimate proving ground. Engineering a complex system like Xet storage is a balancing act. You strategy for scale, performance, and reliability, but once bytes start moving, challenges emerge. The trick is knowing when to move from design and theory to practice.

LFS, the storage system behind repositories today, stores large files in a separate object storage outside of the repository. LFS deduplicates at the file level. Even tiny edits create a new revision to upload in full; painful for the multi-gigabyte files found in many Hub repositories.

In contrast, Xet storage uses content-defined chunking (CDC), to deduplicate at the level of bytes (~64KB chunks of data). If you edit one row in a Parquet file or tweak a small piece of metadata in a GGUF model, only those changed chunks are sent over the wire.

This provides significant benefits to large file transfers. For example, the Xet team keeps an internal ~5 GB SQLite database that powers a metrics dashboard. With LFS, appending 1 MB (around the average patch currently) requires re-uploading the entire 5 GB file. With Xet storage, we push only the newly introduced data.

This means uploads for the dashboard take a tenth of a second (at 50Mb/s) instead of the 13 minutes if the database were backed by LFS.

Making this work requires coordination between the following components:.

Before moving to production, the system was launched into an ephemeral environment, where we built a steel thread of functionality to enable uploading and downloading via the huggingface_hub. The video below highlights our progress one month in:.

After the heady highs of a quick proof-of-concept, the team settled into battling gnarly integration points (privacy, backward compatibility, fragmentation, etc) with the complex ecosystem that is the Hub. Eventually, the infrastructure moved into production for Hugging Face team members. With real usage now rolling in, we moved forward with the first large-scale migration.

According to recent reports, on February 20th at 10 a.m., it was all hands on deck. In the weeks prior the team had built the internal tooling to migrate files from LFS to Xet and, just as importantly, roll back a repository to LFS if necessary. Now it was time to put it to the test. Grafana and Kibana lit up with fresh logs and metrics, showing the load shift in real time.

The picture is the same in Kibana, only here you can tell when we took a lunch break:.

By the end of the day, we had successfully migrated all target repositories for a total of 4.5 TB into Xet storage. Downloads from each repository were now served by our infrastructure.

Industry observers note that no launch is without its lessons. The system handled the load smoothly and migrations went off without any major disruptions, but as the bytes flowed through various components we began to see some trends.

Reviewing network throughput post-migration, we saw that CAS was downloading four times more data than it was returning to clients:.

Recent findings suggest that upon further investigation we found the vast majority of requests to CAS were for 10MB ranges of data within files. These requests come from people that are using hf_transfer to accelerate their downloads of large files. The requested ranges do not align on block boundaries and the block format doesn’t provide uncompressed chunk lengths to facilitate skipping directly to the data within the block. Instead, CAS streams the block starting at the beginning and reads until it finds the requested data.

Sources indicate that given a block with an average size of 60MB and multiple partial requests to ranges within that block, the overhead accumulates. CAS reads 210MB for just 60MB delivered, a ratio of 3.5 bytes downloaded : 1 byte sent to the client. At scale across blocks of irregular sizes and ranges that can span several blocks, the 4 bytes downloaded : 1 byte sent ratio is matched.

As usual, an image is worth a thousand words:.

Industry observers note that to fix this, we updated the block format to store chunk-length metadata, enabling CAS to download only what each request actually needs. This format change required coordinated updates across:.

Sources indicate that all of which were undertaken without downtime. Not only did this result in a balanced ratio in CAS downloads to returned data, but also reduced GET latency by ~35% across the board.

At the same time, we also saw an unexpected load imbalance across our CAS cluster. One pod would spike to hundreds of active uploads while other pods chugged along at single digits. Swapping the load balancer’s routing algorithm (from round-robin to least outstanding requests) and adding more nodes made little difference in the moment.

Digging deeper we realized that during uploads, CAS writes to a temporary file for validation before uploading without calling fsync, allowing the OS to buffer writes in the page cache. When a spike of uploads comes in, the unflushed page cache leads to increased memory pressure.

As the OS tries to flush the page cache to disk, the pod experiences throughput throttling from block storage, causing increased latency on uploads. While uploads slowly process, newly introduced requests continue to come in, pushing more to the disk. This creates a vicious cycle, leading to a backlog of uploads and the imbalance that we saw during the migration:.

To keep a pod from getting in this state, we put a limit to the number of concurrent uploads each machine accepts before rejecting requests that, when reached, pushes requests on to other pods in the cluster. If all pods in the cluster get in this state, then our autoscaling policies kick in. Longer-term solutions might include forcing disk syncs, removing the on-disk buffering, or switching to ephemeral storage with better throughput.

Recent findings suggest that these two issues led to key architectural improvements, but they weren’t the only challenges the team tackled in the weeks following the migration. We also addressed other performance issues, a memory leak (which we fixed but still can't definitively root cause), and on advice from AWS to migrate the LFS Bridge from an Application Load Balancer (ALB) to a Network Load Balancer (NLB) to improve scalability during bursts of traffic.

In short, real-world load was essential for exposing these challenges, and incremental migrations let us tackle them safely. That’s how we’re ensuring Xet-backed repositories scale reliably for the entire Hugging Face community with faster uploads, fewer bottlenecks, and minimal disruption all the way.

With the initial migration complete, Xet is now on the Hugging Face Hub.

We’re finalizing an official integration with the huggingface_hub that will mean you get the benefits of Xet without any significant changes to your current workflow. To get going:.

If you have any questions, drop us a line in the comments 👇 or open a discussion on the Xet team page. And stay tuned as we roll out more pieces (faster web uploads, faster Git workflows), bringing faster big-file collaboration to every AI builder on Hugging Face!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At its annual GTC conference, NVIDIA has unveiled a trio of groundbreaking open-source releases aimed at accelerating physical AI development. Release of a newly introduced suite of world foundation models (WFMs) with multicontrols called Cosmos Transfer, a highly curated Physical AI Dataset, and the first open model for general humanoid reasoning called NVIDIA Isaac GR00T N1 - represent a significant leap forward in physical AI technology, offering developers powerful tools and resources to advance robotics systems, and enhance autonomous vehicle technology.

Cosmos Transfer, the latest addition to NVIDIA's Cosmos™ world foundation models (WFMs), introduces a upcoming level of control and accuracy in generating virtual world scenes.

Available in 7 billion parameter size, the model utilizes multicontrols to guide the generation of high-fidelity world scenes from structural inputs, ensuring precise spatial alignment and scene composition.

The model is built by training individual ControlNets separately for each sensor modality used to capture the simulated world.

Input types include 3D bounding box map, Trajectory map, Depth map, Segmentation map.

Outputs from Cosmos Transfer varying environments and weather conditions.

Cosmos Transfer coupled with the NVIDIA Omniverse platform is driving controllable synthetic data generation for robotics and autonomous vehicle development at scale. Find more Cosmos Transfer Examples on GitHub.

Cosmos Transfer samples built using post-training base model are also available for autonomous vehicles.

NVIDIA has also released Physical AI Dataset, an open-source dataset on Hugging Face for developing physical AI. This commercial-grade, pre-validated dataset consists of 15 terabytes of data representing more than 320,000 trajectories for robotics training, plus up to 1,000 Universal Scene Description (OpenUSD) assets, including a SimReady collection.

The dataset is designed for post-training foundation models like Cosmos Predict world foundation models, providing developers with high-quality, diverse data to enhance their AI models.

It has been revealed that another exciting announcement is the release of NVIDIA Isaac GR00T N1, the world's first open foundation model for generalized humanoid robot reasoning and skills. This cross-embodiment model takes multimodal input, including language and images, to perform manipulation tasks in diverse environments. The NVIDIA Isaac GR00T-N1-2B model is available on Hugging Face.

Isaac GR00T N1 was trained on an expansive humanoid dataset, consisting of real captured data, synthetic data generated using components of the NVIDIA Isaac GR00T Blueprint, and internet-scale video data. It is adaptable through post-training for specific embodiments, tasks and environments.

According to recent reports, isaac GR00T N1 uses a single model and set of weights to enable manipulation behaviors on various humanoid robots, such as the Fourier GR-1 and 1X Neo. It demonstrates robust generalization across a range of tasks, including grasping and manipulating objects with one or both arms, as well as transferring items between arms. It can also execute complex, multi-step tasks that require sustained contextual understanding and the integration of diverse skills. These capabilities make it well-suited for applications in material handling, packaging, and inspection.

Isaac GR00T N1 features a dual-system architecture inspired by human cognition, consisting of the following complementary components:.

Post-training is the path forward to advancing autonomous systems, creating specialized models for downstream physical AI tasks.

Check out GitHub for Cosmos Predict and Cosmos Transfer inference scripts. Explore the Cosmos Transfer research paper for more details.

Sources indicate that the NVIDIA Isaac GR00T-N1-2B model is available on Hugging Face. Sample datasets and PyTorch scripts for post-training using custom user datasets, which is compatible with the Hugging Face LeRobot format are available on GitHub. For more information about the Isaac GR00T N1 model, see the research paper.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that on March 14, we submitted Hugging Face's response to the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy's request for information on the White House AI Action Blueprint. We took this opportunity to (re-)assert the fundamental role that open AI systems and open science play in enabling the technology to be more performant and efficient, broadly and reliably adopted, and meeting the highest standards of security. This blog post provides a summary of our response, the full text is available here.

Open approaches to AI development are not only (typically) more transparent, adaptable, and scientifically sound, they have also consistently reproduced or surpassed the performance of widely-used API-only commercial offerings on many tasks; and are increasingly doing so on shorter timelines, with increased resource efficiency. Our team's recent OlympicCoder outperforming Claude 3.7 on complex coding tasks with 7B parameters and an open-source post-training recipe, or AI2's fully open OLMo 2 models (with open training data) matching o1-mini performances, are two of the most recent compelling examples. These successes show that a robust AI strategy must leverage open and collaborative development to best drive performance, adoption, and security of the technology. We make three major recommendations in this direction.

According to recent reports, the most advanced AI systems to date all stand on a strong foundation of open research (attention mechanisms, transformer architectures, cheaper post-training algorithms) and open source software (PyTorch, Hugging Face libraries, supercomputer operating systems) — which shows the critical value of continued support for openness in sustaining further progress. Investment in systems that can freely be re-used and adapted has also been shown to have a strong economic impact multiplying effect, driving a significant percentage of countries' GDP. As AI systems with open weights and training techniques become increasingly attractive options for developers in terms of both performance and cost, prioritizing public research infrastructure and broad access to compute, customizable models, and trusted open datasets — especially for smaller developers and researchers — will be essential to the further technical and economic success of AI technology.

Industry observers note that addressing the resource constraints of organizations adopting and adapting AI technology will be essential to supporting its diffusion and fostering innovation from adopters across the entire development chain. Smaller models (that may even be used on edge devices), techniques to reduce computational requirements at inference, and efforts to facilitate mid-scale training for organizations with modest to moderate computational resources all support the development of models that meet the specific needs of their use context, especially in high-risk settings such as healthcare where fully generalist models have proven unreliable. More efficient and purpose-designed AI systems facilitate better in-context evaluation, better resource utilization, and enable organizations to build technical capacity at all stages of the AI development chain to ensure that all people can leverage the system that best fits their needs.

Finally, if decades of information security and cybersecurity in open source software are any indication, open and transparent AI systems will have a fundamental role to play in securing AI development and deployment especially in the most critical settings — with different levels of openness needed for different security requirements. Fully transparent models providing access to their training data and procedures can support the most extensive safety certifications. Open infrastructure and open-source tooling implementing the latest training techniques can empower organizations to train the models they need in fully controlled environments. Open-weight models that can be run in air-gapped environments can be a critical component in managing information risks. Prioritizing adoption of the most transparent systems, supporting the development of the open resources outlined, and building capacity to leverage them especially in critical settings of AI adoption are essential to enabling more secure AI adoption.

Please refer to the full response for our more detailed recommendations!

It has been revealed that AI-generated videos are becoming an important part of modern web design. Designers can now create animated backgrounds, product demonstrations, hero section videos, and visual storytelling elements without relying entirely on traditional video production. However, generating a visually appealing video is only one part of the process. To use AI-generated videos effectively on a website, developers and designers must also understand video formats, visual quality, file optimization, and website performance.

These technical factors directly influence how videos appear across devices, how swiftly pages load, and how smoothly visitors interact with a website.

In a recent development, video format selection is one of the first technical decisions when preparing AI-generated assets for the web. Different formats offer different levels of compression, compatibility, and visual quality.

The most commonly used formats include:.

For most websites, MP4 with H.264 remains a dependable default. WebM or AV1 can be offered as additional formats where appropriate.

Developers should also consider browser compatibility before selecting a format. Providing multiple sources allows browsers to choose a supported option.

In a recent development, AI-generated videos can sometimes contain visual inconsistencies, unnatural movements, distorted objects, or changes in lighting between frames. These challenges become more noticeable when videos are displayed in large website sections.

Industry observers note that resolution is an important factor in maintaining visual quality. Common resolutions include:.

However, higher resolution does not automatically mean better website performance or user experience. A 4K video may look impressive, but loading it unnecessarily can increase bandwidth consumption.

Sources indicate that frame rate also affects the viewing experience. Many website videos work well at 24 or 30 frames per second. Higher frame rates may be useful for fast-moving scenes, but they also increase the amount of visual data that needs to be processed.

Designers should review AI-generated footage before publishing it. Checking transitions, motion consistency, sharpness, and color accuracy helps prevent distracting visual problems.

Sources indicate that large video files can significantly increase website loading times. This is especially crucial for websites with video backgrounds, animated landing pages, and multiple visual sections.

Video optimization involves reducing file size without making the footage noticeably worse.

Some practical optimization techniques include:.

Compression: Video compression reduces unnecessary data while preserving notable visual details. Developers can use encoding tools such as FFmpeg to adjust bitrate, resolution, and codec settings.

In a recent development, bitrate control: Bitrate determines how much data is used to represent each second of video. A higher bitrate generally preserves more detail but increases file size. Selecting an appropriate bitrate depends on the video's resolution, movement, and intended display size.

It has been revealed that trimming unnecessary footage: Website videos rarely need to be several minutes long. Removing unused sections helps reduce file size and keeps visual content focused.

Removing unnecessary audio: Background videos that do not require sound should be exported without an audio track. This reduces unnecessary data and supports a cleaner user experience.

Responsive video delivery: Websites should serve appropriately sized assets for different screen sizes. A smaller video may be sufficient for mobile users, while desktop visitors can receive a higher-resolution version.

These techniques help developers balance visual quality with efficient content delivery.

Industry observers note that even a well-optimized video can affect website performance if it is implemented incorrectly. Developers should consider how videos are loaded, displayed, and processed by browsers.

Industry observers note that for example, automatically loading several large videos when a page opens can consume significant bandwidth. Instead, developers can use lazy loading strategies for videos that appear further down the page.

For background videos, the HTML video element offers several useful attributes:.

A simple implementation looks like this:.

According to recent reports, developers should also avoid autoplaying large videos unnecessarily. A static image can often provide a better experience on mobile devices or slower connections.

Performance testing tools such as Google Lighthouse and Chrome DevTools can help identify whether video assets are affecting loading speed, bandwidth usage, or rendering performance.

Industry observers note that technical optimization should not come at the expense of accessibility. Background videos should not distract people or make website content difficult to understand.

Developers should respect the prefers-reduced-motion media query, which allows users who prefer reduced animation to receive a less motion-intensive experience.

A suitable static background image can be displayed as an alternative.

Mobile compatibility is equally crucial. Smaller screens, limited data looks, and varying network conditions can make heavy video assets less practical. Testing videos on different devices and connection speeds helps identify potential problems before publication.

AI-generated video assets offer exciting possibilities for modern web design, but their successful implementation requires more than creative output. Choosing suitable video formats, maintaining consistent visual quality, compressing files, and considering website performance are all essential parts of the development process.

It has been revealed that by combining thoughtful video production with responsive delivery, accessibility considerations, and performance testing, designers and developers can create engaging websites without compromising loading speed or usability. As AI video technology continues to evolve, understanding these technical fundamentals will remain valuable for building efficient and visually appealing web experiences.

The best AI humanizer for web content is the one that changes how a draft reads without changing what it states. If you need a specific tone, Humanize Max gives you four styles and three lengths in one run. If you already work in QuillBot or Grammarly, their humanizers fit the account you have. GPTinf, Humanize AI and Undetectable AI put an AI check next to the rewrite, and Ahrefs gives you quick variants of a short passage.

To compare them on equal terms, we ran the same 103-word AI-written release note through each tool in November 2026. It contains a product name, two image formats, a settings path and the word "must", so it shows whether a tool keeps the details a reader acts on. We also checked every feature, limit and price on the vendor's own pages on the same day.

A humanizer earns its place only if its output needs fewer fixes than the draft you started with, and these six checks show whether a tool will do that for your content.

Humanize Max is a single-purpose humanizer: you paste an AI draft, upload a file or load the built-in sample, choose a style and a length, and get a rewritten version in a few seconds. The four styles are Academic, Casual, Creative and Formal, and the three lengths are Shorten, Standard and Expand, so you can turn a stiff feature description into casual blog copy and trim it in the same run.

The result highlights every phrase it changed, which makes it quick to check whether a product name or a settings path came through. If the rewrite doesn't land, Run it again produces a different version of the whole text. At the time of writing, it takes up to 2,000 words per run and works without an account.

Pricing: Looks and limits are still being finalized, so check the site for current terms.

Best for: Rewriting AI drafts of blog posts, product pages and emails into a specific tone.

QuillBot's AI Humanizer sits next to its paraphraser, grammar checker and AI detector, which makes it a natural pick if you already use QuillBot for rewording. Basic mode is free for up to 125 words per run, while Advanced mode, which rewrites more deeply, comes with Premium (the pricing page also lists three Advanced uses on the free plan). In our test, it asked us to create a free account before it showed the first result.

Premium removes the word limit and adds Freeze words, which keeps the terms you choose unchanged, along with tone insights, a history of past runs and a Chrome extension that humanizes text inside ChatGPT and Gemini.

Pricing: Basic mode is free. Premium is listed at $8.33 a month, billed annually.

Best for: Quick fixes to a paragraph or two for writers who already use QuillBot.

GPTinf is a writing toolkit built around its humanizer, with an AI detector, plagiarism checker, grammar checker, paraphraser and readability checker on the same site. The humanizer has two modes, Standard and Academic, and takes pasted text or a PDF, Word or plain-text file. File-to-File mode returns the humanized document in its original format, so a long brief keeps its layout.

It has been revealed that custom Style lets you paste 150 to 1,200 words of your own writing, and later runs are shaped to match it, with no account needed. After each run, an AI-likelihood estimate appears under the output, so you can see whether a draft needs another pass. Treat that number as a probability, not proof of who wrote the text.

It has been revealed that pricing: A free proposal is available. Paid plans start at $9.99 a month for Lite (5,000 words), with Pro at $24.99 and Unlimited at $59.99.

Best for: Freelancers and content teams that want to rewrite and check drafts without switching tools.

Grammarly's AI Humanizer comes in two layers. The tool on its web page is free, works without an account and offers basic humanization of pasted text or an uploaded document. A free Grammarly account adds the Humanizer agent, with four preset styles, a custom voice built from a writing sample, and support for English, Spanish, French, German, Portuguese and Italian.

Sources indicate that grammarly claims the humanizer focuses on clarity and readability rather than on AI detectors, which matches how most web teams use these tools. If you need to show how a piece was written, Grammarly Authorship shows which parts came from AI, which came from online sources and which you wrote yourself. The basic tool's word counter allows up to 1,500 words per run.

Pricing: The basic humanizer is free. Grammarly Pro is listed at $12 on the looks page, which doesn't state the billing period.

Best for: Teams that already write in Grammarly and want one voice across documents.

Humanize AI is built for people who want to tune the output. Without an account you get the Free tone, a Rewrite level slider with three stops (Quality, Balanced and Max) and Custom style, which learns your voice from 150 to 1,200 words of samples. A free account opens eight more modes, including Formal, Informal, Academic, Expand and Shorten, and on desktop a Writing level menu sets how plain or dense the result reads.

Industry observers note that view changes highlights every edit, and File-to-File accepts PDF, DOCX, TXT and MD documents and returns them in the same format. Paid looks also include a public API that supports the same styles and rewrite levels as the web app, so a developer can add a humanizing step to a CMS or publishing pipeline.

Pricing: Paid intends start at $9.99 a month for Lite (10,000 words), with Standard at $19.99 and Unlimited at $59.99. Yearly billing lowers the monthly price.

Best for: Teams that need precise tone control or want to humanize text through an API.

In a recent development, undetectable AI keeps its humanizer simple: one text box, one button and no style or length settings. Its free allowance works differently from the others, with 1,000 words in total before you need an account and another 1,000 once you create a free one.

Sources indicate that under the output, a Check for AI button runs a detection check on the result, and the same site has a separate AI detector and plagiarism checker. Its FAQ says pasted text isn't published or shared but doesn't say whether it's stored, so keep confidential details out of the drafts you run through it.

According to recent reports, pricing: Paid plans start at $9.99 a month for Lite (5,000 words), with Pro at $25 (25,000 words) and Unlimited at $59 (1,000,000 words). Yearly billing lowers the monthly price.

Best for: Trying a humanizer on a full-length draft before you commit to an account.

Ahrefs, best known for its SEO platform, offers a free AI Text Humanizer among its writing tools. You paste up to 2,048 characters, choose one, three or five variants, and pick the version that reads best. It ran without an account in our test.

Variants are the useful part. For a hero headline, a meta description or a product blurb, comparing three rewrites side by side is faster than prompting a chatbot three times, and you can export all results as a text file. The character limit, which fits a few short paragraphs, rules it out for full articles.

Pricing: Free on Ahrefs' website.

Best for: Short marketing copy where you want several options to choose from.

The best AI humanizer tool for a documentation team isn't the one a growth marketer needs, so match the tool to the content in front of you.

There isn't one winner, because these tools solve different problems. The quickest way to decide is to run a paragraph from your own work, ideally one with a product name, a number and an instruction, through two or three of the tools above, and keep the one whose output you'd publish with the fewest fixes.

Sources indicate that google's guidance on using generative AI content is about value rather than the tool: mass-producing pages that add nothing for readers can count as scaled content abuse. A humanizer changes phrasing, not usefulness, so the same rules apply. Google also recommends fact-checking AI-generated titles, meta descriptions and image alt text before you publish.

It has been revealed that the best humanizer for your team is the one whose controls match your content: tone presets for blog posts, variants for short copy, change highlighting for docs and a custom voice for marketing. Run one of your own paragraphs through two or three tools from this list, then read every highlighted change, especially names, numbers and words like "must", before anything goes live.

Recent findings suggest that gradio’s gr.Dataframe component is one of our most popular components, we've seen it used in a variety of awesome apps, like leaderboards, dashboards, and interactive visualisations. Although we hadn't made any changes to the dataframe in quite some time, our backlog of complications had been growing, and some improvements had been in demand for a while.

According to recent reports, well — we’re now super excited to release a host of new updates to Gradio’s dataframe component. Over the last 6 weeks, we’ve closed over 70 dataframe issues - including bugs, improvements and enhancements.

You can select multiple cells at once! Copy or delete values across your selection with ease.

Recent findings suggest that add row number columns and keep critical columns in view while navigating wide datasets using the pinned_columns parameter. No more losing track of what you're looking at!

Industry observers note that easily copy cell values into a comma-separated format with our latest copy button. Need a better view? The full screen button gives you interactivity without distractions and can be enabled with the show_full_screen parameter.

According to recent reports, look at all that data! Now we can just scroll to the top.

Recent findings suggest that improved keyboard navigation makes gr.Dataframe more accessible than ever. You can also take control of your dataframe’s look with a dedicated styler parameter and enhance the user experience of your app.

Access entire row data in select events for more intuitive interactivity and data manipulation.

Customise the interactivity of your dataframe by specifying non-editable columns using the static_columns parameter.

Quickly find the data you need with our powerful search feature by setting the show_search parameter to "search".

Narrow down your dataset to focus on exactly what you need with flexible filtering options with show_search set to "filter".

Experience smoother, more intuitive cell selection that behaves the way you expect.

With over 70 issues closed, we’ve made huge improvements, but there’s always more for us to work on. Looking ahead, we still have more ideas to implement and we’re excited to keep refining accessibility, performance, and integration. Look out for some cool demos on our socials using the dataframe on Gradio’s X.
